summary: Lands the Desk v2 stack tip (e0ad62ad, bot-06-quality-security/desk-v2-assembled-prompts) onto main as one draft PR. The tip was 17 ahead / 39 behind main because PRs #17-#24 were squash-merged into intermediate stack branches only. Rebased those 17 commits onto origin/main rather than merging, so each seat's commit and authorship survives and no already-merged stack parent is rewritten. Two add/add conflicts resolved by hand. One real regression found and fixed: main's #16 tightened G-4 and the tip's change document predated the new rule.

strategy.why: The 17 tip commits are linear and only 2 of them touch a file main also changed, so a rebase resolves conflicts twice rather than collapsing seven seats' work into one merge commit. Rebase replays the tip onto main; it does not rewrite the stack branches, which still point at the original commits.
strategy.rejected: A merge commit would have preserved the same content but buried the per-seat attribution that G-1 and G-2 read, and would have made the per-commit ownership replay below impossible.

auto_merged: ownership.yaml — main's 23 added rules plus the tip's 3 (scripts/generate-templates.py to LEAD, ci/tests/** and ci/.github/** to QUALITY). Additive on both sides.
skills/README.md — main's agent-bus row (#14) plus the tip's 7 Desk v2 skill rows.
ci/.github/workflows/gates.yml — main's hardened template plus the tip's G-7 step.

hand_resolved.resolution: Kept main's reviewed document (#27) as the spine and folded in the tip's three new sections: tool rosters, tool packs, versioning. Corrected main's claim that contracts/ is committed 'empty-of-product' — true of api/ and events/, no longer true of the directory, now that tool-rosters/ and tool-packs/ hold real contracts. Added both to the Layout block.

Kept main's version entirely and added only the tip's G-7 step. The tip's copy of this file was an OLDER snapshot of the template that predated main's #12-#15 hardening: it carried `--bot "${{ steps.bot.outputs.bot }}"` interpolated into run:, `RECEIPT=$(ls -1 ".receipts/${{ ... }}"/*.json | head -n1)`, an unanchored `^bot-0[0-6]-` regex, and no `if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'`. Taking the tip side would have reintroduced exactly the two shell-injection P1s QUALITY flagged. Built the file as main's comment header plus the template body verbatim, which is what .github/workflows/gates-template-sync.yml requires.
hand_resolved.dropped: The tip's pre-hardening gate body. Every rule it expressed is present in main's body; only the unsafe interpolation is gone.

The acting bot is now derived from the GITHUB_HEAD_REF / GITHUB_REF environment variables rather than a ${{ }} expansion, validated against `^bot-0[0-6]-[a-z0-9-]+$` (anchored at both ends), and passed to later steps through an env: block as "$BOT". No ${{ }} appears inside any run: body in either gates.yml.

security_findings_carried_forward.title: g5/g6 approval_id is never verified against any approval record
security_findings_carried_forward.verdict: VALID and systemic. No approval record exists anywhere in the gateway; rosters.py only checks that a gated tool's SCHEMA requires the field, never the value. Every g5/g6 tool across Play, App Store, Vercel and Railway accepts any string and echoes it back, where it reads as an audit trail. approval_id='full' satisfies the 100 percent production check.
security_findings_carried_forward.disposition: NOT FIXED — deliberately. A real fix needs an approval store, an issuance path with an answer to who approves and how they authenticate, single-use scope-bound consumption, and new tools, which is a contract change. That is a feature and SYSTEMS'/LEAD's design call; inventing it inside a landing PR would put an unreviewed authorization mechanism into the security-critical path, and a partial fix would look like security without being any.
security_findings_carried_forward.residual: OPEN. Proposed shape recorded on the review thread. Pre-existing from PR #22 and unchanged by this landing. Does not block the file-level landing; should block pointing real Play or App Store credentials at this gateway.

observations: PRs #17-#24 were squash-merged into intermediate stack branches rather than into main, which is how main came to lack services/desk-gateway, contracts/tool-rosters, grokbot/, infra/desk-gateway and skills/desk-bootstrap while all eight PRs read as merged. Worth a note in the stack procedure: a squash-merge into a branch that never reaches main leaves the PR green and the repository unchanged.

The tip carried an older copy of .github/workflows/gates.yml than main did, so a naive 'prefer the tip' resolution would have silently reverted the #12-#15 shell-injection hardening on the live workflow. main's gates-template-sync.yml is what makes that recoverable: because the live body must equal the template body, the correct resolution is mechanical rather than a judgement call.
G-4's surface-coverage rule from #16 will do this to every change document written before it. Any other stack branch still waiting to land should expect the same failure and the same one-line fix.

The template-sync check cannot catch this class on its own: it compares the two copies to each other, so it passes when both are equally vulnerable. That is exactly what happened — the tip carried an older copy of both files forward and sync stayed green. TestWorkflowShellInjection checks each file against the property rather than against its twin, which is the gap that let the regression through.

Greptile reviewed the rebased tree and found six issues in code that PRs #17-#24 had already reviewed and approved in their own PRs. Four were contained bugs, now fixed. One (G-7 tolerating missing generated artifacts) is a deliberate, explicitly tested decision, not a defect. One (unverified approval IDs) is a real design gap left open on purpose. Worth noting for the stack procedure: reviewing eight PRs separately did not surface what reviewing the assembled result did.

Greptile's P2 on the first version of these tests was right: they ran a transcribed copy of the bot-resolution script, so a change to the workflow's parsing could leave them green. Reproduced that exact scenario before rewriting them — the copy-based tests pass against a workflow whose guard has been unanchored, as long as the pattern text survives somewhere in the file. The tests now extract and execute the shipped step. A test that cannot observe the thing it names is worse than no test, because it is counted as coverage.

Greptile caught the same mistake twice in this PR, in two different files: a test that asserts on a helper rather than on the code path that calls it. The workflow-injection tests ran a copy of the bot-resolution script; the traversal tests asserted safe_path directly and would have passed against a handler that never called it. Both now execute the real path. The pattern worth remembering: when a fix is 'call the existing guard', the test has to prove the call happens, because the guard itself was never broken.
